268.title: How to measure AI adoption in a large company
268.short: A systematic approach to assessing AI Adoption inside a large company: from solution architecture to a detailed breakdown of the methods applied. Attendees will get a framework for evaluating the effectiveness of AI initiatives, allowing them to manage the process of neural network adoption based on data.
268.description:
How to assess the success of AI process adoption. Without clear metrics, AI transformation risks turning into blind hype that brings no measurable benefit to the business. The talk examines a systematic approach to assessing AI Adoption inside a large company: how to measure what many consider unmeasurable.

The speaker will break AI transformation down into specific areas and draw the boundary between what really lends itself to digitization and what cannot be measured. You will see how the analytics of AI Adoption at Nebius is structured from the inside: from solution architecture to a detailed breakdown of the methods applied. Drawing on the experience of successful corporate transformations in BI, Lean and Kaizen, the speaker will show not only working mechanics, but also break down his own mistakes, honestly highlighting situations in which standard approaches do not work.

As a result you will get real examples of metrics and analytics that can be immediately transferred to your own business. The talk will give product managers and CPOs a transparent framework for evaluating the effectiveness of AI initiatives, allowing them to manage the process of neural network adoption based on numbers rather than intuition

269.title: Antifragile metrics: when analytics starts to drive decisions
269.short: The main result of analytics is expressed not by the accuracy of numbers, but by which decisions the company makes on their basis. What to do when familiar product metrics have stopped reflecting the long-term health of the product, and different teams understand differently what exactly counts as success? You will learn how to change the approach to product measurement and influence real business decisions

270.title: Optimization traps: when uncoordinated decisions make the overall result worse
270.short: Game theory for analysts. In his lecture on game theory, Alexey Savvateev will explain the Nash equilibrium concept in accessible terms and show through a series of examples how the interaction of selfish participants can lead to a collective loss. Braess's paradox, the prisoner's dilemma, the tragedy of the commons — in all these situations equilibrium logic does not guarantee a satisfactory outcome from the standpoint of the global benefit to society. Particular attention will be paid to how changing the rules of the game changes people's behavior, which must be taken into account when designing incentive schemes. No special mathematical background is required, but a willingness to reason will come in handy.

271.title: Mind outside the head: from the stone hand axe to artificial intelligence
271.short: How our brain created knowledge and how the artificial information environment affects it, when AI changes the cultural environment faster than human biology.
271.description:
Mind was not a predetermined goal of evolution — human intelligence emerged and developed not only inside the brain: tools preserved ways of acting, language transmitted experience, social groups accumulated knowledge, and writing and digital technologies created humanity's external memory.

One of the main amplifiers of human intelligence was the transmission of knowledge — language, imitation, teaching and a long childhood made cumulative culture possible. Human history is the history of external carriers of mind, and if earlier tools mostly stored and retrieved knowledge, generative systems are starting to assemble answers, offer explanations and take part in decision-making.

Stanislav Drobyshevsky traces this trajectory from stone technologies and the origin of speech to writing, digital data and generative models. Why was intelligence not an inevitable goal of evolution? How did cooperation help sapiens turn individual experience into culture? Which abilities do we gain and lose by handing memory and thinking over to external tools? And what can anthropology really say about humans in the age of AI?

This is a lecture about how the biological brain created an external world of knowledge and how the artificial information environment affects it, when AI changes the cultural environment faster than human biology

272.title: A/B tests on employees: from AI copilots to sales scripts
272.short: The specifics of testing AI copilots and other internal products and company processes, in order to answer precisely the question "did the new tool change employees' work enough to make scaling it worthwhile".
272.description:
Internal products — AI tools, telephony, sales scripts — require experimental validation, but classic A/B testing breaks down quickly here. Instead of millions of independent users you have dozens or hundreds of employees, where the test group talks to the control group and the results depend on team structure and incentive systems. The talk examines the experience of Avito Sales Tech in running A/B tests of internal products on small fixed samples (dozens of managers).

The speaker will show how to get a statistically reliable causal answer under strong, specific network effects. You will learn how to choose the level of randomization (employee, team or work period) and what price the move from individual to team-level testing carries.

We will go through working with small samples: group balancing, use of the pre-period, CUPED and validating the design on historical A/A tests. A separate block covers accounting for external factors: how to separate the learning period for a new tool from a lasting effect and how to factor in current incentives and motivation (KPI).

Attendees will learn to design informative experiments even on dozens of employees. The talk will provide a framework for evaluating internal AI solutions, CRM and processes: how to build a causal chain from a workflow change to a business effect. You will understand why access to a tool does not mean exposure, and how to correctly link growth in intermediate work metrics to the resulting economic benefit when deciding whether to scale a product

273.title: It's not all that good: what an A/B test doesn't tell us about users
273.short: How a deep analysis of an A/B test audience helps find unexpected experiment effects, make more precise product decisions, and improve the quality and accuracy of recommendations.
273.description: A/B tests help make product decisions, but average experiment results do not always reflect what is happening with individual user groups. In the talk we will look at a content platform case and show how a deeper look at the audience helps find unexpected experiment effects and make more precise decisions about product development. And also how this affects the way content that suits a particular user profile is recommended
lectorRoles: Head of the ML analytics team, VK (Dzen)

274.title: How to calculate the cumulative effect of a series of experiments: measuring the impact of ML improvements on product metrics
274.short: Retrospective assessment of the cumulative effect on the product from a series of consecutive experiments. Methods for estimating the cumulative effect and when a counterfactual scenario is necessary.
274.description: Retrospective assessment of the cumulative effect on the product from a series of consecutive experiments. Methods for estimating the cumulative effect and when a counterfactual scenario is necessary
lectorRoles: Analyst in the recommendations and search group, VK Музыка, VK

275.title: How to measure the effect of product changes without an A/B test?
275.short: In our case we cannot split sellers into groups A and B: that would mean giving different sellers different promotion conditions. So a classic A/B test is impossible. The solution is synthetic control: it makes it possible to measure the effect of changes without directly splitting sellers into test and control groups
275.description:
E-commerce platforms constantly experiment with internal promotion algorithms and pricing. However, when testing minimum ad rate thresholds, a classic A/B test turns out to be legally impossible: randomly splitting sellers into test and control groups means giving them different commercial terms, which directly violates antitrust law. This creates a deadlock: how do you measure price elasticity and test product hypotheses when classic user randomization is strictly prohibited? The talk covers RWB's experience of estimating causal relationships under hard constraints using the synthetic control method.

The speaker will show the internal mechanics of the tool: changes are rolled out not to individual sellers but to entire product categories. You will learn how regression models based on "donor categories" with similar historical behavior are used to predict a synthetic control trend for the test group. Special attention will be paid to testing statistical significance in complex non-parametric approaches — Kuramagomed will walk through the math of calculating it via a permutation test to estimate the real incremental effect of a price change.

Listeners will get a detailed "in plain terms" explanation of how the synthetic control method works and will understand its mathematical connection to the popular Difference-in-Differences approach. The talk will give product analysts and data scientists a ready-made framework for legally and statistically valid testing of pricing hypotheses where standard A/B platforms are completely powerless.

276.title: The pitfalls of LLM labeling in effect estimation
276.short: Review sentiment, contact topic, product category — until recently all of this was labeled by hand, and now it is labeled by language models. Along with that, the status of the numbers computed on such labeling has changed. The dashboard metric and the experiment's target metric are no longer observed — they are predicted. Can you compute statistics on a metric that a model assigned, and what is wrong with that statistics?
276.description:
Handing the classification of texts (sentiment, topics, categories) over to language models made labeling fast and cheap. However, along with this the status of the numbers the business sees on dashboards changed: the target metric is no longer observed directly but predicted. The industry tends to assume that checking the classifier's overall accuracy is enough to launch a pipeline, but in practice this approach leads to fundamental distortions in the estimation of product and marketing effects.

The talk examines the mathematical nature of the error in neural-network labeling: the model does not err randomly but where the text is harder. The bias in a share depends on the share itself, so data from different segments is not comparable, and if the difficulty of texts changes over time, a dynamics that does not exist appears in the metrics. The speaker will show why in A/B tests classic randomization does not save you from a distorted measurement of the outcome. You will learn how an LLM classifier can compress a real effect, depriving the experiment of its built-in statistical power and invalidating the MDE calculation. Separately, the popular myth that a consensus of several different LLMs guarantees reliability will be dismantled (spoiler: their errors are often correlated).

Attendees will get a rigorous statistical method for correcting these distortions based on prediction-powered inference. The talk will provide a ready algorithm: how, using a small manually labeled validation sample, to estimate and subtract the model's bias. You will learn how to build a pipeline in which the unbiasedness of the final estimates is guaranteed by the sampling design rather than by the quality of the neural network itself.
lectorRoles: PhD in economics, researcher at the Faculty of Economics, MSU, expert in causal inference econometrics and experimental methods

277.title: How a single SQL query can show that your attribution is lying to you
277.short: The speaker shares SQL code that lets you check whether your attribution model is honest on your own data, plus a faster marker of incorrect source evaluation in one-touch models. Attendees will get a reusable analytical framework for quickly quantifying problems with one-touch attribution, which distorts the real contribution of advertising channels in B2B products and services with long deal cycles.
277.description:
In B2B products and services with a long deal cycle, standard one-touch attribution models (first touch / last touch) predictably distort the real contribution of advertising channels. At M2, the hypothesis that such models were inadequate led to an attempt to implement multi-touch attribution. However, instead of a classic story of successful development, the speaker will walk through a case where building a multi-touch model initially failed — but it was precisely this failure that exposed fundamental problems in the traffic evaluation system.

Instead of weeks of designing custom algorithmic models, the team spent only two days on diagnostics using a standard stack: the Yandex Metrica Logs API and any DBMS. The talk examines the logic of this research in detail. The speaker will show the specific SQL query used in the study and will also share an even faster marker that your standard attribution models are evaluating sources incorrectly. This is an engineering breakdown of how to "cut the corner" and cheaply verify the problem without over-engineering and ML models.

Attendees will get a reusable analytical framework for quickly quantifying problems with one-touch attribution. The talk will show how the results of this short study at the level of raw logs forced the business to reconsider its strategy: to stop scaling classic performance acquisition and shift focus toward brandformance. You will take away a ready-made SQL template that lets you check the honesty of your current attribution on your own data

278.title: How to turn thousands of conversations into data marketing can make decisions on
278.short: Transforming raw voice logs into structured datasets with neural networks. We build automatic transcription, intent tagging and emotion recognition to turn speech into data suitable for quantitative analysis
278.description:
Traditional qualitative analysis of customer communications does not scale: manual call listening covers only a small share of dialogues. As a result, a mass of unstructured information (objections, insights, behavior patterns) remains a blind spot for analytics. The talk examines a method for transforming raw voice logs into structured datasets using neural networks. On a dataset from the UIS platform, the speaker will show how to build automatic transcription, intent tagging and emotion recognition in order to turn speech into metrics suitable for quantitative analysis.

The talk is based on a detailed breakdown of three applied business cases. First: parsing a mass of calls to identify real objections, which made it possible to rebuild product pages and double the conversion to inquiries on current traffic. Second: building a process for predictively identifying dissatisfied customers, which reduced the number of negative reviews by 70%. Third: a 6% increase in success conversion through adjusting scripts based on semantic analysis. The speaker will justify the methods used and examine the operational limitations of AI models: transcription cost, accuracy problems in specific niches, and the team's own mistakes during implementation.

Attendees will learn how to build a pipeline for turning unstructured speech into tabular data for research. The talk will provide an understanding of the methodology: how to correctly tag calls and link speech analytics data to business results. You will understand which tasks machine dialogue analysis is economically justified in, and which — where it fails and requires manual validation or classic research methods.

279.title: Evaluating the effectiveness of “flight” offline advertising
279.short: A step-by-step guide to assembling a Bayesian MMM for “flight” placements and a model diagnostics checklist. A breakdown of working with adstock (the effect of fading memory of advertising) and saturation (diminishing returns on investment)
279.description:
When it comes to evaluating marketing effectiveness, analysts are used to relying on high-frequency digital channel data. However, the harsh reality of large brands is a complex mix of digital and offline, often launched in “flights” (bursts) with weekly aggregation. As a result, after three years of active campaigns you have only about 150 rows of data. Under such conditions, classic ML (linear regression, XGBoost) breaks down and produces negative weights for channels that actually work, while time-series models (Prophet) err in forecasting during a flight-based advertising campaign and do not answer the main business question — “what drove the sales?”

The talk breaks down in detail the process of building marketing mix models (MMM) based on Bayesian regression — an approach that lets you extract the maximum of insights from a minimal amount of information. The speaker will justify why this particular mathematical apparatus saves you in conditions of data hunger and will show how to integrate business rules directly into the model through prior distributions (priors). In practice, you will work through how to correctly program adstock (the effect of fading memory of advertising) and saturation (diminishing returns on investment).

As a result, you will take away a step-by-step guide to assembling a Bayesian MMM for “flight” placements. The talk will arm you with an exhaustive model diagnostics checklist: from purely statistical metrics (like R-hat) to calibration on external data and sanity checks. You will learn to build offline advertising evaluation models in a way that the business will finally believe.

280.title: A metric for media advertising: why it is sometimes better to build new than to change the old
280.short: A new data model makes it possible to build a flexible attribution window, link media impressions with Metrica goals and AppMetrica events, and add new parameters and traffic-quality metrics.
280.description:
Media advertising has historically suffered from fragmented data: classic analytics tools struggle to connect upper-funnel impressions with final conversions, especially when the user journey crosses web and mobile apps. When the old system's architecture stops coping with cross-platform tasks and strict attribution limits, the business faces a choice: endlessly refactor the legacy or design the base from scratch. The talk covers the experience of the Yandex team, which chose the radical path of rebuilding the architecture.

The speaker will break down the design of the new data model in detail and show how abandoning the old logic made it possible to implement a truly flexible attribution window. The main focus of the talk is the mechanics of stitching disparate signals into a single user journey. You will learn how, under the hood, a seamless link is built between raw media impressions, goal actions from classic Metrica, and in-app events from AppMetrica, providing conversion transparency regardless of platform.

A separate block will be devoted to extending the analytics toolkit on the new architecture. Listeners will see how the built-in flexibility allows enriching data with custom parameters and introducing advanced traffic-quality metrics. The talk will help data team leads make informed decisions about rebuilding internal analytics platforms, and will give analysts an understanding of how to transparently assess the impact of top-of-funnel campaigns on final revenue.

281.title: The anatomy of churn in SaaS products: 9 cuts that show the real reason customers leave
281.short: Approaches and methods for analyzing cohorts, plans, lifecycle stages, behavior, reasons for leaving and more.
281.description:
Customer churn is often perceived by the business as a single flat metric, which inevitably leads to wrong product decisions. Treating churn rate as an unambiguous evil hides the real dynamics: looking at the overall number, a company cannot see the difference between failed onboarding, a downgrade by loyal users and the natural departure of a non-target audience. The talk breaks down a research approach to deep churn segmentation that lets you find the true points of revenue loss in SaaS products.

The speaker will present a methodology for decomposing churn into nine key analytical cuts. You will learn how to properly cross-analyze cohorts, pricing plans, lifecycle stages and the behavioral patterns of churning users. The mechanics of working with qualitative data on reasons for leaving will be shown, along with ways to link it to quantitative product metrics. Special attention is paid to the concept of «good churn» — situations where losing a customer is mathematically and strategically good for the business, and attempts to retain them bring more losses than value.

Listeners will get a ready-made analytical framework for diagnosing churn. The talk will help move from passively watching an overall figure to targeted work with segments: you will start to clearly understand which users need to be won back by any means and which are better let go.
lectorRoles: Chief Customer Office, Dynamic Yield and Algolia (IT consulting)

282.title: Managing ad traffic during periods of high utilization
282.short: When utilization is at its peak, you cannot show the business multiple-fold growth, nor give partners the required volumes at the expense of free traffic. We share our utilization calculation methodology, approaches to media planning and ways to cool down traffic.
282.description: When a site's ad inventory hits the utilization ceiling, the classic extensive monetization model breaks down. The business keeps demanding multiple-fold revenue growth by inertia, advertisers expect the usual volumes, but there are simply no free impressions left. An attempt to aggressively grow inventory leads to audience burnout and a drop in efficiency, while refusing partners leads to lost budgets. The talk covers Magnit AdTech's experience of managing a Retail Media ecosystem under a severe shortage of free capacity.

283.title: Data catalog as a product: how to digitize data flows and close key user scenarios across the business
283.short: Turning a data catalog from a "registry of tables" into an internal product at the ecosystem level, building an architectural frame, and then "sewing" into it the logic that closes real user scenarios of analysts, engineers and data owners.
283.description: How to turn a data catalog from a "registry of tables" into an internal product at the ecosystem level: digitize the main data flows and objects across the holding, build an architectural frame, and then "sew" into it the logic that closes real user scenarios of analysts, engineers and data owners. Which product principles are important in this process, how to build synergy of functions and how to scale data management.

285.title: A mission-based model for order clustering
285.short: We cluster tens of millions of baskets and show that instead of clear missions there is a continuum with anchors. We explain how to separate the purpose of an order from basket size and discount, which quality metrics to compute before A/B and why we moved from clusters to the «occasion × product group» matrix
285.description:
A beautiful idea: all orders fall into clear clusters. In reality there are no clusters, only a continuum of order purposes — not clouds at a distance from each other, but one complex figure with density clusters — «anchors».

We went through a hierarchy of basket representations and saw how these anchors manifest. And how their names drift: «Sweet gift» in June turns into a bag of charcoal for a barbecue, at graduation parties into chocolates, around New Year into alcohol. «For my beloved self» means toilet paper, cat litter and mosquito repellent.

We will tell you how to build such a model on your own data, which quality metrics to compute before A/B and why we did not turn it into a production tool. And where we went next: to the «occasion × product group» matrix and new levers for raising ARPU
lectorRoles: Head of Commercial Analytics, Магнит Доставка

286.title: When PSM no longer works: moving to system dynamics simulation models
286.short: A system dynamics simulation model calibrated to actual business metrics, answering the question of what will happen to the metrics if business parameters are varied.
286.description:
Estimating the economic effect of business expansion under limited resources is a complex task, since classic A/B testing does not work here. In the Yandex.Drive case, opening new service zones in a city with a shared fleet inevitably led to cannibalization of old zones. Running a per-user test is impossible because of network effects, and using switchback experiments (by geo and time) leads to the opened geography starting to unpredictably “flicker.” To bypass these limitations, the team developed an approach to experimentation using a synthetic control group. A carsharing simulator — a system dynamics simulation model — is used as the synthetic control group, acting as the control group.

The talk covers the simulator's architecture and the process of calibrating it to actual business metrics. The model describes the equilibrium between demand, car availability, conversion, orders, and fleet utilization. You will learn how, with such a simulator, to forecast changes in key indicators: total revenue, dynamic profit, car idle time, and revenue per car-day when varying business parameters (geography, average check, order duration). The speaker will justify the use of simulation modeling in conditions where other incrementality evaluation methods are inapplicable, and will highlight situations in which this approach does not work.

Listeners will learn how to apply system dynamics to estimate revenue increment and sales cannibalization. The talk will show the process of creating a test environment that allows forecasting the behavior of complex systems under changes in external conditions (for example, how the first snow will affect demand and the SLA of the delivery service). As a result, you will get a working tool for tuning dynamic pricing algorithms and dealing with excess supply in services with shared resources.

287.title: Finding suspicious patterns in user behavior
287.short: How antifraud analytics turns behavioral and content signals into product restrictions, how their effectiveness is measured, and how to evaluate detector quality on historical data.
287.description:
Using a hypothetical case of spam in comments on public posts, we will look at how an analyst can identify suspicious user behavior. We will talk about how to look for behavioral and technical signals, formulate rules for detecting spam, test them on historical data and evaluate the quality of triggers. We will separately discuss the trade-off between missed violations and false positives, and also why one rule is not enough and how violators' behavior can change in response to restrictions.

The case will be based on synthetic data and illustrate the analytical process rather than building an antifraud system from scratch.

288.title: AI agents: how progress becomes everyday practice (and where you can already do without a subscription)
288.short: Working scenarios without a subscription to Claude Code, Codex and other cutting-edge solutions. Which tasks are solvable right now on a fully open stack, and where limitations remain. Experiments with Goose, Qwen and DeepSeek
lectorRoles: Lecturer at MIPT, expert in multimodal data analysis

289.title: How AI is changing BI: where we stumble, what works and where we run next
289.short: Dashboards stop being someone's job, while semantics and context have not yet become someone's job. How BI at Авито lived through 2026 in this fog: data content certification, domain AI readiness, skills and knowledge bases, prerequisites for an AI analyst, solved and unsolved problems. No success stories, but with a therapeutic effect
289.description:
Dashboards stop being someone's job, while semantics and context have not yet become someone's job. The focus of BI has shifted from «a factory of reports as products» to governance, metrics and the knowledge graph. Self-service BI has been reborn as agentic self-service.

I will tell how at Авито we lived through 2026 in this fog, what we changed over the year and which expectations turned out to be overestimated. I will break down why certification of marts, metrics and dashboards has returned to focus and whether everyone can afford the prerequisites of an AI analyst. I will show how we grow the AI readiness of domains through federated data governance, metadata generation and a network of BI partners. There will also be problems that we cannot solve yet.

A talk without success stories, but with a therapeutic effect. It is for BI developers, leads and heads who do not yet feel new ground under their feet, those who are deciding what to do with BI in the AI world. You will compare your vision with the experience of Авито, take away working ideas and leave with the feeling that you are not running in the fog alone.

290.title: How much analytical work can be handed to an agent and how to verify it is done
290.short: Eight steps from an analytical task to an accepted agent answer with checks at different stages: transferability is determined not by the complexity of the task, but by whether the decisions it requires are declared; an undeclared decision will still be made — by a layer, a mart or a model; acceptance depends on the image of the result, and acceptance itself has a blind spot.
290.description:
The use of AI analysts is becoming a mass trend, but there is almost nothing to verify their work on real data with: without a manual duplicate query, the correctness of a calculation is not confirmed. So you can approach from the other side — not "what the agent can do", but "what needs to be done with the task, the data and the scaffolding so that a correct answer becomes more likely".

The result is a framework of eight steps from statement to accepted result, and at each step there is a check and a typical failure that occurs regardless of model and domain.

A live analytical backlog is laid out by image of the result - what appears when a task is closed: a number, an export, a dashboard, a pipeline cell, an edit to a report, a study, an agreement on a metric definition, an A/B test.

The first conclusion: transferability is determined not by the complexity of the task, but by whether the decisions it requires are declared. An undeclared decision will still be made: by a layer, a mart or a model, each time anew. And declaring is not enough. Between "we described this" and "the agent sees this" lies the scaffolding, and it loses: a significant part of the decisions recorded in model comments and tests does not reach the agent's context, and including a layer with table descriptions in one of the measurements actually narrowed the input.

Hence the second conclusion, less obvious: the answer is not the only outcome of the work.

An agent can stop and list what is missing, and each non-answer has its own party to blame: the framing of the question, the absence of an object in the data, the semantic layer, or the discipline of recording results.

It turns out that not everything is fixed by prompt and context.

Work must be accepted by image of the result: a number has its own truth, an export has another — a set of rows and a control aggregate, a study has none at all, and there the stability of the conclusion is checked, not correctness.

The talk examines several techniques with measured boundaries: comparison with a known answer, decomposition of a number into summands, checking that nothing extra was affected, addition in two ways, reading what the agent decided itself, recalculation with a different decision.

Attendees will get a sequence of actions that raises the share of correct answers, and a way to check each step for themselves: whether the declared decisions reach the agent, what changes in the input when a layer is enabled, and what to accept each image of the result with.

And separately - how to check your own check.
lectorRoles: Head of product analytics for commercial products, Samokat.tech

291.title: The pretrain data factory: how to turn the web, documents, audio and video into a training corpus
291.short: Data quality control at big tech scale without manual labeling and the specifics of preparing media sources. The architecture of a pretrain corpus preparation pipeline and a checklist of what to cut off so as not to burn expensive compute on dirty data
291.description:
When a model is trained on a complex mixture of web, images, audio or video, data preparation stops being a set of one-off scripts. It turns into a large-scale engineering product — a "data factory" with a continuous stream of raw sources at the input and a standardized training corpus at the output. The talk examines the construction of an end-to-end conveyor that replaces disparate scripts with a unified architecture for collecting, cleaning, deduplicating, filtering and packaging data for all modalities.

The speaker will break down in detail the structure of a multimodal pipeline based on distributed systems. You will learn how to control data quality at industrial scale without manual labeling, using extraction algorithms, automatic classifiers, scoring and heuristics. The audience will break down at which stages the cost of computation grows nonlinearly, and how to correctly prioritize sources so as not to spend unique resources on low-quality data.

As a result you will get a reference architecture of a pretrain corpus preparation pipeline, ready to be adapted to your tasks. You will see how to assess the labor intensity of processing different modalities already at the planning stage, combining strict data engineering with project management.

292.title: How much context does AI really need?
292.short: We will compare how AI works with a database schema, data, technical metadata and a full semantic layer. We will look at which part of business context AI can recover from the schema and the data itself, and which part it must be given explicitly by the company, without turning the construction of a semantic layer into a multi-year project of describing the entire company.
lectorRoles: Head of the analytics and data infrastructure department

293.title: Is the analyst market overheated or do candidates just not know how to sell themselves?
293.short: We'll honestly break down what is actually valued in interviews and how to stand out among other candidates. We'll talk about salaries, strange company requirements and matching with the future team. We'll find out where it's better to grow as a specialist, where to go for money, and what matters more when choosing an offer: title, interesting tasks, people or salary.
293.description:
The product analytics market often seems overheated, and the employment process — opaque. Candidates face a string of rejections, inexplicable salary spreads on identical positions and strange hiring conditions. The talk examines the underside of job hunting in IT: without abstract advice and stories of "successful success", exclusively on the basis of real interviews, salary negotiations and one's own mistakes.

The talk examines in detail the process of evaluating vacancies and employers. The speaker will explain why financial conditions on similar positions differ drastically, what actually hides behind loud job titles, and how to stand out among competitors. The audience will break down the typical screw-ups of hiring companies and the non-obvious red flags one can encounter in an interview, including specific cases from big tech.

Attendees will learn how to objectively assess their value on the market and not measure professionalism by the number of rejections. The talk will give a list of questions about tasks, processes and conditions that must be asked of the hiring manager before accepting an offer, in order to choose a job by real substance rather than by the signboard.

294.title: How to manage the probation period and what is wrong with it
294.short: A candidate sold themselves perfectly in the interview, but it turned out that something was off and they need to be fired. What to do if HR does not agree to fire based on the results of the probation period, but you don't want to be a hostage of the situation either.
294.description:
The probation period was conceived as a legal tool to protect the business from hiring mistakes, but in practice it often turns into a legal trap. The situation where a candidate brilliantly sold themselves in the interview but completely failed the real tasks is familiar to every manager. However, an attempt to part ways with such an employee regularly runs into the resistance of the HR department, which blocks dismissal under the article because of the high risks of labor disputes. As a result, the hiring manager becomes a hostage of their own mistake and is forced to drag along an incompetent specialist. The talk examines the legal and management mechanics of safely parting ways with employees who have not passed probation.

The speaker will show how to set up the process of assigning tasks and control so that dismissal becomes a predictable procedure rather than a stress for the whole company. You will learn how to correctly formalize expectations in the first days of work, correctly record intermediate results and assemble an ironclad evidence base of non-conformity to the position held. Separate attention is paid to the algorithm for interacting with internal lawyers and HR staff: how to argue your position, remove colleagues' fears about inspections and formalize the parting without the slightest litigation prospects for the employee.

Attendees will get a strict management framework that allows turning the probation period from a paper formality into a really working filter. The talk will give leaders a clear toolkit for protecting their interests, so as to quickly and legally clean the team of unsuitable people without damage to work processes and the employer brand.
lectorRoles: Director of the HR management department, Cordison

295.title: What AI-harness is and why the system matters more than a specific model
295.short: Setting up the scaffolding and MCP servers to automate routine work. A breakdown of scaling mistakes, operational limitations and the tasks where LLMs absolutely must not be left unchecked
295.description:
The drive to take routine load off analysts (ad-hoc queries, incident investigation) often runs into the complexity of setting up and maintaining AI tools. In the Uzum Market case, the team came to use Opencode as a tool that covers 90% of routine tasks with minimal effort. As a result, every stakeholder got a "$100-a-month junior analyst": just enter credentials to the needed systems, and all permitted skills, MCPs and models appear as a single web interface.

The talk examines in detail the technical implementation and architecture of such an AI Harness: how to deploy it on a small server in just a week and ensure full controllability. The speaker will show the transformation of work processes: Uzum analysts no longer write SQL queries by hand, 90% of dashboards are created by agents from scratch (from a Jira task to the final visual), and investigating DAG failures takes minutes. Scaling mistakes, operational limitations and tasks where LLMs absolutely must not be left unchecked will also be examined.

Attendees will learn how to choose and configure scaffolding and MCP servers to automate routine work. The talk will give concrete advice on introducing the tool into teams and help analysts move into the role of leaders of mini-teams of AI agents, multiplying the speed of qualitative research.
lectorRoles: Team Lead of marketing analytics, Uzum

296.title: Democratizing data access in the AI era: how to build a semantic layer in a company from scratch
296.short: Designing a semantic layer and integrating it with Looker. Covers operational constraints, non-obvious technical challenges and our own mistakes.
296.description:
Moving to AI analytics is impossible without a single dictionary of metrics. If algorithms are let straight into the raw tables of the corporate warehouse, the business gets neural network hallucinations and discrepancies in key metrics. The foundation for data democratization is a semantic layer that translates business terms into strict logic that both LLM agents and ordinary employees can understand. The talk uses the example of the Careem superapp infrastructure to break down the process of designing such a layer from scratch.

The speaker will show how a micro-team of three people deployed an MVP of the semantic layer on the open-source Cube platform and proved to the business that the approach works. He will talk about the technical architecture of the solution and the nuances of integrating with Looker. Hamid will separately address the buy vs build choice: which tools are worth paying enterprise cheques for, and what is more profitable to build in-house (a comparison of Cube, Looker and Superset).

The main part of the talk is devoted to rollout under high load: operational constraints and technical difficulties that appear when the whole company gets access to data. Hamid will break down the process mistakes of the Careem team that any data function will face when connecting AI to a real warehouse. As a result you will get a blueprint for building a semantic layer where manual control by the data team remains only where automation cannot replace it.

297.title: Analytics data architecture for an AI product: how to get rid of lags on billions of events
297.short: A proven scheme for building high-load pipelines for preparing ML datasets, crawling and ETL. How to embed business logic in the data model, and why abandoning streaming aggregation of global states makes the system resilient
297.description:
Building analytics under extreme loads often leads to incidents. The talk examines a production case from Sber: the system processed a stream of 200 thousand events per second with an accumulated base of half a trillion records. An attempt to compute URL state aggregations "on the fly" via a Materialized View in ClickHouse led to Too many parts, a halt of backfill processes and the formation of a lag of a billion events in the main realtime loop.

The speaker will break down this architectural mistake in detail and show how the incident forced the team to completely rebuild the system. You will learn why the business requirement to "see the metric quickly" does not mean realtime computation. The audience will study a batch loop of four layers (Raw → State → Mart → History). We will break down how to compute the historical state of an object from a compact State layer instead of reading the entire base of raw events, and how to publish a mart atomically so as to free dashboards from the "flickering" of incomplete data.

As a result you will get a proven way of building high-load pipelines for preparing ML datasets, crawling and ETL. The talk will give clear criteria: when complex analytics must be moved into a separate batch loop, how to embed business logic in the data model, and why abandoning streaming aggregation of global states makes the system resilient.

298.title: A systematic approach in agentic coding: how to be sure this is a working product without reviewing tens of thousands of lines of code
298.short: A working bundle of open-source tools for agentic coding. The OpenSpec and OpenSpec+ development methodology. Turning chaotic generation into a predictable and controlled engineering process.
298.description:
A systematic approach in agentic coding: how to be sure this is a working product without reviewing tens of thousands of lines of code

The speaker will break down approaches to creating products with agents and show a working bundle of open-source AI coding tools. The solution is based on the OpenSpec development methodology and its improved version OpenSpec+. You will learn in which situations this bundle works and in which it does not, and why the main price for product quality is a multiple increase in token consumption.

Listeners will get a set of ready-made recipes for your harness, capable of rebuilding the stochastic process of AI code generation into a controlled engineering process.
lectorRoles: Chief data analyst, IT holding T1

299.title: The leader's AI operating system: an architecture of 17 roles and 13 procedures
299.short: How to turn work with LLMs into a sustainable management method and optimize the managerial decision-making process
299.description:
Managerial decision-making amid frequent shifts in priorities requires rethinking the basic operational routine. The talk examines an engineering approach to personal management: creating an AI operating system based on autonomous agents. This is not a set of disparate prompts, but an architecture consisting of 17 roles with clear competence boundaries and 13 regular procedures embedded in the real daily work of the director of an analytical function.

The speaker will break down the mechanics of the system in detail. You will learn how a radical reduction in the cost of management procedures changes the decision-making process: for example, a preliminary breakdown of a task that previously required two hours and was often ignored now takes 30 minutes and is always performed algorithmically. The audience will study the structure of "rehearsal panels" — AI profiles of real stakeholders that allow running an argument through criticism before a meeting. A separate block is devoted to an automatic context layer that deterministically loads goals, current focus and open threads into every session. The speaker will also break down system failures, including an incident where four independent agents generated a convincing but completely false conclusion.

Attendees will get a scheme for assessing the cost of their own management procedures in order to transfer them into the AI loop. The talk will give concrete mechanics for assembling the context layer and setting up isolated AI critics for preparing for reviews, difficult 1-1s or budget defenses. As a result you will learn how to turn work with LLMs from chaotic requests into a sustainable management method whose architecture has proven its viability both in an enterprise environment and in the production of a medtech startup.

300.title: The price of a result: how we stabilize contact cost at Avito?
300.short: What we do to make pricing at Avito fairer for the seller by optimizing contact cost.
300.description: What we do to make pricing at Avito fairer for the seller by optimizing contact cost
lectorRoles: Senior analyst on the pricing team, Avito

301.title: How we built analytics in an AI assistant for sellers
301.short: We parsed the "black box" of seller-assistant dialogues, even without using LLM judges. We managed to fully build funnels of recommendation execution, identify the main user scenarios for using the assistant and measure the quality of the AI assistant.

302.title: How to send communications so as not to overspam users and turn this into a system
302.short: We turned mass CRM pushes into a system that automatically adjusts the volume and composition of the audience to the balance of supply and demand on the part-time work platform. We break down the path from calculating segments and prioritizing users to verifying the solution with an A/B test. As a result, users began receiving six times fewer pushes without a decrease in the number of shift bookings.

303.title: Monetization feed on the home page: a dozen iterations and an uplift we did not believe
303.short: The cross-category monetization feed on the home page is one of the most lucrative rollouts of the monetization efficiency team. I'll tell how we learned to bring quality paid traffic from the home page. Separately I'll break down the main lesson for analytics: why in A/B tests that change ranking, a per-user split inflates the revenue effect many times over, how we caught this and measured it.
