304.title: An analyst as a team lead of AI agents: three AI engineering cases, from channel scoring to dashboard development
304.short: We turn AI from a code generator into a managed executor capable of taking a task from a vague business question to a verifiable result.
304.description:
In agentic analytics, a senior specialist often becomes the bottleneck: they have to get up to speed in a new industry, reconstruct logic from documents, design a methodology, write SQL and verify the result. Generating code via LLM speeds up only a small part of this process, leaving the main problem — context handover and control over metrics. The master class covers the next stage in the evolution of the AI-first workspace: how to turn AI from a code generator into a managed executor capable of taking a task from a vague business question to a verifiable result.

The speaker will walk through three real production cases. First: an audit of a pharma company's ad placements (12 million visits), where the agent built a pipeline for UTM normalization, metric calculation and scoring of 56 segments. Second: a product CJM funnel for a fintech, where the agent designed an MVP of ClickHouse marts taking into account the identity bridge and checks for user stitching conflicts. Third: oversight of an external Power BI developer, where the agent reconstructed requirements from meeting transcripts, prepared DAX instructions and audited the finished report, finding critical errors in the data grain and LTV calculation.

Listeners will learn how to reformat their backlog for delegation to AI agents and build a "context → plan → implementation → verification" loop. You will learn to turn documents and data schemas into reusable context, define hard boundaries of delegation and fix acceptance criteria for automated checks, so that you can safely make business decisions based on AI work

305.title: Building a Discovery pack for testing product hypotheses
305.short: Assembling agentic systems that deliver results of stable quality. An engineering breakdown of components and architecture patterns for AI solutions.
305.description:
In a workshop based on Yandex Ai Studio we will assemble a multi-agent system for running fast product research — from idea to reporting presentation:

- We will create an assistant for formulating hypotheses

- We will create a researcher agent for the market and competitors

- We prepare skills for processing research data — generating a Lean Canvas, User Story Map, wireframes

- We create a presentation generator

- We will set up quality control points (Human-in-the-Loop)

By the end of the workshop attendees will understand how to assemble agentic systems that deliver results of stable quality, which components and patterns the architecture of AI solutions is built from, and where AI can actually speed up a product manager's work and where the automation's output needs validation.
lectorRoles: Head of strategic projects, Yandex AI Studio

307.title: How to strengthen a marketing department with AI agents in practice
307.short: How agents run Yandex.Direct, generate content and design, build analytical dashboards and perform marketing tasks on schedule.
307.description:
The introduction of AI into marketing often comes down to point-by-point generation of images and texts, but the real breakthrough happens when agents take control of the full 360° contour of tasks. In this reality, strong marketers transform into operators of agents, multiplying efficiency many times over, and routine processes are automated. The master class examines the real experience of IT-Agency in a deep restructuring of marketing production with the help of AI agents.

The speaker will show the inner kitchen of the project: from organizing the Shared Workspace and designing the knowledge base (KPI, target audience, budgets) to integrating AI tools (Codex, Claude, Cursor) via API with advertising systems. We'll break down the architecture of end-to-end management: how agents run Yandex.Direct, launch SMM, generate content and design, build analytical dashboards and perform tasks on schedule. This is an honest engineering breakdown: in addition to the architecture and justification for the stack choice, you will learn about operational limitations, costs, the team's own mistakes and situations in which this approach absolutely must not be applied.

As a result you will get a step-by-step algorithm for moving marketing onto AI rails. The master class will give a clear understanding of how to set up the environment, connect channel APIs and restructure processes so that a small team manages the workload of a full-fledged department

309.title: AI for market intelligence: how to automate demand, market, and competitor research
309.short: We turn a chain of analytical steps into an automated process: forming queries, analyzing dynamics, and using the results to test product and marketing hypotheses. How a multi-step search agent works — one that forms queries, studies results, returns to search, and collects information from many sources — and how to turn typical competitive research from a manual process into repeatable agentic research.
309.description:
Market research, demand analysis, and competitive analysis still require a lot of manual work: formulate dozens of search queries, collect data from different sources, study competitors' websites, compare products and prices, and then pull it all together into a single conclusion. AI agents make it possible to change the very approach to this work. Instead of individual LLM queries, you can assemble a research workflow in which the agent independently formulates search tasks, calls external tools and data sources, analyzes the results, refines the search, and forms final conclusions. In the talk, practical cases will show how this works: from an agent with Wordstat MCP for demand analysis to a Deep Research agent for multi-step internet research and automated competitive analysis. We will also look at which tasks are already worth delegating to AI and where an analyst is still essential.

Listeners will get answers to the questions: how AI agents turn a chain of analytical steps into an automated process; how an agent can independently work with search demand data — forming queries, analyzing dynamics, and using the results to test product and marketing hypotheses; how a multi-step agent works that forms search queries itself, studies results, returns to search, and collects information from many sources; and how to turn typical competitive research from a manual process into a repeatable AI workflow.

310.title: Marketing AI-native analytics: from on-site behavior to money in the till
310.short: I will show how to build marketing AI analytics on top of what you already have running, without breaking integrations. We will assemble calls, deals and web analytics from telephony, Битрикс24, Roistat, PostHog and Метрика into a single loop. We will build a customer path graph in Neo4j: from the first click to the deal. An AI agent will process thousands of touchpoint chains and answer the key business question: «On which segments are you losing money, and where do you actually earn it?».
310.description:
The task that was solved: put data about the customer's path and behavior into one database, describe it with entities, build on top a graph «key query → visit → session → conversation with a salesperson → deal» and place an AI agent above it so that a manager could ask questions about the customer path themselves, without a queue to an analyst.

Stack: telephony with speech analytics, Битрикс24, Roistat. PostHog session replay, Метрика Logs API, BigQuery, Neo4j Graph. The listener will get a working method for building marketing AI analytics from scratch: collecting user data, consolidating it into one platform and providing the AI agent with an environment where the full picture is visible. During the lecture a working environment and live queries will be demonstrated, including the places where the data link broke and what had to be redone.

311.title: Custom analytics: how an AI agent speeds up the path from business question to result
311.short: A scheme for embedding an AI agent into the request-processing pipeline, with automated quality control and important human checkpoints. We break down the solution's architecture, the logic of automated data quality tests, typical mistakes and the agent's operational limits
311.description:
The main bottleneck in handling ad-hoc requests is often not writing SQL code but translating a business statement into a strict analytical task. Every unrecorded agreement about filters, cuts and constraints generates new rounds of discussion and returns for recalculation. To solve this problem, the Veborama team built an AI agent. On input it receives an unstructured request in business language, and on output it produces a complete package of artifacts: a formalized statement of the task, a list of metrics, a data work plan and a draft SQL code.

The agent is integrated on top of the company's existing data landscape, including available marts, ELT modules and a library of automated validation rules. It does not replace the analyst but acts as a preprocessor: it surfaces ambiguities in requirements at an early stage and prepares a set of checks relevant to the specific request. Using a real case, the talk breaks down the architecture of this solution, the logic of automatic selection of data quality tests (integrity, event sequence, anomalies), as well as typical mistakes and the agent's operational limits.

Attendees will get a scheme for embedding an AI agent into the request-processing pipeline, including automated quality control and human checkpoints. The talk will show the measurable effect of formalizing tasks through AI: a lower share of returns for rework, time saved on data preprocessing and a multiple increase in analyst throughput.

312.title: A seamless event analytics migration: moving product analytics from AppMetrica to our own event stream
312.short: Our own event stream instead of AppMetrica — and the minimum requirements for event data so an LLM agent can start answering data questions with no human in the loop.
312.description:
Off-the-shelf analytics solutions like AppMetrica handle basic reporting well, but when moving to AI analytics they hit a natural barrier. For an autonomous LLM agent to answer ad-hoc business questions correctly without a data engineer involved, the company needs absolute control over the quality, naming and structure of raw logs. The talk breaks down the experience of the «Магнит Плюс» team in moving product event analytics from a third-party tracker to its own event stream.

The speaker will show the engineering underside of a large-scale event analytics migration. You will learn how to design the architecture of an in-house solution and ensure a seamless move without breaking current product dashboards. Special attention is paid to the process of automatic validation of the new data stream against the old one and to syncing the tracking logic on the fly.

The main focus of the talk is on preparing infrastructure for artificial intelligence. You will get a breakdown of the minimum requirements for event data: exactly how event structure and metadata need to be set up so that the neural network can confidently navigate the warehouse and give the business accurate answers under automated quality control instead of a human in the loop. Listeners will take away a roadmap for moving to their own pipeline and a checklist for data readiness for integration with LLM agents.
lectorRoles: Head of Digital Services Analytics, Магнит Плюс

323.title: Taking control of the dark side of AI: security, privacy and AI firewalls when working with LLMs
323.short: Banning ChatGPT is easier than learning to work with it safely. Positive Technologies' chief infosec evangelist Alexey Lukatsky explains how Russian companies build secure workflows with Western LLMs. In the lecture we will look at data anonymization methods, the architecture of AI firewalls and, most importantly, how a product analyst can learn to negotiate with the cybersecurity department so that the favorite phrase "infosec won't approve this" becomes the start of a productive dialogue rather than a cross over AI adoption.
323.description:
Alexey Lukatsky has more than 35 years in cybersecurity, 18 of them at Cisco and now at Positive Technologies. He has been an encryption developer, an infosec admin and an evangelist, so he understands perfectly why product analysts and security people often speak different languages. While the business demands fast insights and widespread AI adoption, the information security department responds with its usual "ban it".

The talk is about moving the use of neural networks out of shadow IT and into a legitimate channel. We will talk about how Russian companies actually solve the issue of working with Western LLM models without the risk of leaking trade secrets and sensitive user data.

Alexey will cover the engineering side of the question: how modern methods of anonymizing datasets before sending them to an external cloud work, what AI firewalls are and how they filter prompts and model responses. The talk will help analysts understand the logic of professionally cautious people from security, learn to discuss risks under tight deadlines and make a reasoned case for the architecture of their AI solutions before internal infosec review.

324.title: Corporate AI security: the architecture of constraints and the vulnerabilities of user scenarios
324.short: Deploying AI does not protect against leaks if, for the sake of speed, a user copies the whole trade secret into the prompt and grants the app access to the entire disk. The talk examines the architecture for restricting AI services' access to corporate data and two vulnerability mechanisms: providers' open logs and the transmission of hidden instructions into active sessions. The speakers will show how to build a "green corridor" for typical tasks, introduce AI solution passports and test security through simulation of work processes.
324.description:
Even after corporate AI is officially rolled out and training is conducted, data leaks continue. Facing tight deadlines, employees tend to optimize their work at the expense of security: they copy a manager's assignment in full, along with closed financial terms, and give third-party AI services excessive access to the whole work disk instead of selecting specific files. A copy of confidential information is created on the external provider's side at the moment of transfer, that is, long before any actual cyberattack. The talk is about moving from a formal ban to an architecture that limits what AI assistants can do at the hardware and process level.

The talk examines technical leak mechanisms in detail using two scenarios: access to stored copies (exposure of database logs, on the DeepSeek example) and data extraction inside an active session (the RovoBlast vulnerability). The speakers will show how to build a perimeter in which an employee's right to read a document does not mean the AI application's right to receive and process it. The process of configuring the target logic will be covered: token control, management of the actual access scope (restriction to specific files) and monitoring of request logs. Separately, the course of action for the security team when data transfer has already happened is considered.

Attendees will learn how to design a "green corridor" for securely performing typical tasks and how to record the rules in an AI solution passport (owner, data sources, available actions). The talk will give a methodology for secure prompting: how to split a request into generating the document structure and the subsequent addition of sensitive numbers in a protected environment. You will get a framework for testing employee skills through simulation of work processes with dummy data, which makes it possible to assess how secure the work really is, and not just whether blocks fired.

325.title: Why does AI draw wrong conclusions from data?
325.short: Delegating analytics to AI does not save you from fundamental errors in statistics. The creator of the VWO stats engine, Ишан Гоэл, breaks down the 5 main traps of data interpretation: from the illusion of averages to the paradoxes of A/B testing and the balance of false positive errors. You will learn which questions to ask any analytical report (generated by a human or a neural network) so as not to take a beautifully formatted but mathematically wrong hypothesis at face value.
325.description:
Data-driven decisions turn out to be wrong far more often than companies are willing to admit. The main reason lies not in processing tools but in a lack of statistical intuition: algorithms generate numbers, and people draw wrong conclusions from them. The talk examines the problem of blind trust in reports and algorithms through the prism of five fundamental errors of analysis.

The speaker, who developed the statistical engine of the VWO platform and taught data analytics to the editorial team of The Economist, will use live examples to break down source distortion and the null hypothesis trap, when absence of evidence is taken as evidence of absence. Special attention is paid to how the cost of false positives and false negatives should directly drive product decisions. You will learn which critical anomalies are hidden behind averaged metrics, and why the chance of randomly getting a winner in an A/B test is mathematically not equal to the probability that the winner is false.

Listeners will get a set of frameworks for checking any analytics (machine or manual). The talk will help data analysts, product managers and marketers develop an intuitive understanding of statistics without diving deep into formulas and will teach them to ask the right questions that break down wrong conclusions in dashboards.

326.title: Adoption, Harness, Knowledge - three drivers of the apocalypse
326.short: How can the whole company go from "AI, help me write SQL" to "AI, take the task entirely"? I'll tell you which technical solutions we assembled for this in our division at Yandex and how we tied them into a single system. In my story we'll break down three drivers of AI usage growth: Adoption — so that people start using AI. How to remove all barriers and make AI a familiar working tool. Harness — so that the agent uses internal tools. How to give the next-token predictor the ability to use the utilities people use and teach it the necessary skills, and then also verify the result. Knowledge — so that the agent understands the context of your business. How to give the agent information about data, code, and company documentation so that you explain less from scratch and don't fill up the entire context window. I'll show how this ecosystem is structured: from interfaces for working with agents to documentation testing. At the end we'll assemble everything on the example of a typical analyst task, and you'll be able to try this architecture on your team and understand which components you're still missing.
326.description:
The transition of a company from basic use of neural networks in the "write an SQL query" mode to delegating full-fledged analytical tasks requires systematic infrastructure. Simply providing access to a chatbot does not make a team more effective: agents lack an understanding of data specifics, access to corporate systems and seamless integration into work processes. The talk examines the experience of Yandex's BigData division in designing a unified technical ecosystem that allows AI agents to autonomously solve complex tasks.

The speaker will break down the system architecture through three key drivers. The first — Adoption: eliminating infrastructural and process barriers to turn a neural network into a basic daily utility for every employee. The second — Harness: endowing the token predictor with real capabilities through access to internal tools, teaching specific skills and automatic verification of work results. The third — Knowledge: integrating agents with the code base and corporate documentation, allowing deep business context to be conveyed without overflowing the LLM's context window.

Attendees will see the entire technical process of assembling the pipeline: from designing interfaces to setting up automatic documentation testing. Using the example of a classic analyst task, it will be shown how these three components work together in a single bundle. The talk will give technical leaders a ready-made framework for auditing their own AI infrastructure and understanding which architectural details the team lacks to move to fully autonomous agents.
lectorRoles: Head of the BigData department, Yandex

327.title: The new transformation of marketing
327.short: We'll talk about how to achieve a measurable result today in areas where quite recently people relied "on faith", how to build an AI-native marketing framework and why a revolution rather than an evolution is needed here. I'll talk in detail about what concrete examples of marketing mechanisms at Avito look like and share life hacks that bring results.
327.description:
Classic marketing long relied on metrics the business simply had to "believe", leaving a wide zone of brand and reach campaigns outside strict analytical evaluation. Today, attempts to improve old approaches point by point yield no result — the transition to fully measurable marketing requires not a smooth evolution but a radical restructuring of processes. The talk examines Avito's experience in implementing an AI-native framework that allows achieving transparent ROI where intuition and qualitative assessments used to rule.

The speaker will show the internal mechanics of Avito's new-generation marketing processes. You will learn how to build the architecture of AI-native marketing, digitize previously unmeasurable channels and connect creative initiatives with hard business indicators. Separate attention will be paid to the practical side of the transformation: the speaker will use concrete examples to break down exactly how algorithms change the team's routine tasks, and will share proven life hacks that already bring a measurable result.

Attendees will get a ready-made management framework for rebuilding the marketing function. The talk will give marketing directors, product managers and analysts a clear understanding of how to abandon "blind faith" in numbers and build a system where every ruble invested is tracked with mathematical precision.

328.title: How we moved to an ai-native state in the data analytics vertical and what it cost us
328.short: Transformation of the data analytics vertical into an AI-native state. Attendees will learn about the "fast-track" for transformation aimed at a radical reduction of the t2m of solving tasks without loss in quality. We'll break down in detail the target infrastructure architecture for an AI-native team, the competencies needed for success and how to deal with rejection of the paradigm shift by the team
328.description:
The development of products like GigaChat sets an extreme pace: classic approaches to analytics simply do not work here because of the speed of change in the industry. To keep up with the product, the data team needs to radically reduce the Time-to-Market (T2M) of solving tasks while maintaining a strict quality bar. Moving an entire analytical vertical into an AI-native state solves this problem, but in practice runs into serious infrastructural barriers and psychological resistance from employees. The talk examines Sber's experience in systematically restructuring data analytics into an AI-oriented format.

The speaker will present a proven transformation fast-track that allows avoiding the classic mistakes of pioneers. You will learn what the target infrastructure architecture for an AI-native team looks like and which new competencies become critically important for analysts. A separate focus will be on change management: Evgeny will honestly tell how to deal with rejection of the paradigm shift inside the team, when employees refuse to trust agents and sabotage new processes.

Attendees will get a step-by-step trajectory for moving their departments onto AI-native rails. The talk will help analytics leaders and CDOs objectively assess the current maturity level of their infrastructure for entering such a transformation and understand what real economic effect and acceleration to expect at the finish.

329.title: Agentic Engineering for Data Tasks Automation
329.short: I'll talk about how we organize end-to-end automation of typical data tasks: how the work of departments changes with the arrival of agents, and how we managed to achieve a 73% speedup on tasks performed by agents. Separately we'll discuss how to calculate the value of AI agents and what to focus on at the organizational level in order to move forward with the agentization of typical data work processes.
329.description:
We all discuss a lot about implementing AI in the IT SDLC. At the same time, about 30% of the labor intensity is taken up by data transformation tasks and the creation of data products. Finding data, assembling a mart, building a dashboard, checking quality, writing documentation — while these processes are performed manually, it is too early to talk about an AI-driven organization and autonomous processes.

I'll talk about how we organize end-to-end automation of typical data tasks: how the work of departments changes with the arrival of agents, and how we managed to achieve a 73% speedup on tasks performed by agents. Separately we'll discuss how to calculate the value of AI agents and what to focus on at the organizational level in order to move forward with the agentization of typical data work processes.

330.title: When an agent becomes an analyst: what will happen to the profession and the team?
330.short: What the near future of analysts will look like, when report and insight factories have already earned their reputation, the analyst is no longer a "bottleneck", and the volume of company context is finite for building an analytical system
330.description:
The introduction of AI agents is changing the fundamental economics of the analytical function. It is no longer about simply speeding up SQL writing — agents take on the entire technical cycle: from data collection to building a report and writing a draft of conclusions. In practice this leads to a radical shift: if previously 80–90% of a specialist's time went to technical work and only 10–20% to communication with the customer, now this ratio is trending toward 50/50. The analyst stops being a bottleneck in report generation, but faces a new physical limit — the need to validate the many times larger volume of ready-made machine insights.

The talk, using the example of a real implementation of agent systems in two companies, examines the next inevitable stage in the evolution of data teams — the transition to an "insight factory", where the business can communicate with the analytical system directly. The speaker will break down the mechanics of transferring repeating corporate knowledge to the machine. You will learn how to digitize a finite volume of context (metric definitions, relationships between tables, access restrictions) so that the system autonomously gives reliable answers to typical questions.

Attendees will get a management forecast and a plan for adapting the backlog for their teams. The talk will help leaders and senior specialists understand how many people will be needed to support data infrastructure in the new paradigm, and how to restructure processes in order to direct the freed-up time to checking complex product hypotheses and creating new solutions.
lectorRoles: Head of AI & RnD, VERA Systems

331.title: AI agents in analytics and Data Science: an architecture on banking cases
331.short: We break down the architecture of an agent system: the task contract, agent management, data and tools, calculations and checks. I'll show how the task, calculation results and check statuses are transferred, when rework is needed and where a human makes the decision. On our cases I'll break down ambiguous metrics, the link between model quality and business KPIs and the impact of drift. The checks will cover data, the applicability of the method, the validity of conclusions and the robustness of recommendations to assumptions: rules and recalculation, the agent searching for contradictions, review by a specialist. I'll show how we plan to apply the architecture in Alfa-Bank's experimentation and Data Science platform
331.description:
Introducing AI agents into industrial analytics and Data Science processes requires a strict architectural base. If you hand a business task to a neural network without strict boundaries, the cost of a mistake can turn out to be critical. The talk examines the engineering scheme of an agent system based on Alfa-Bank's experience: from drawing up the task contract to managing agents, routing data and choosing tools. Special emphasis is placed on synchronization points — exactly how calculation results are transferred, in which cases the process is sent for automatic rework, and where the decision is made by a human with no alternative (human-in-the-loop).

The speaker will use real banking cases to show the mechanics of working with ambiguous metrics, the link between ML model quality and business KPIs and the impact of data drift. You will learn how to build a multi-level system of checks: from the validity of the source data and the applicability of the chosen method to the robustness of the final recommendations to the initial assumptions. Ivan will break down in detail the process in which the agent itself looks for logical contradictions in its conclusions before passing the result to a specialist for review.

Attendees will see how this architecture is embedded in Alfa-Bank's experimentation and Data Science platform. The talk will give data team leaders and DS engineers a ready-made framework for launching their own pilots, allowing them to accurately estimate the expected financial effect of introducing agents taking into account the costs of tokens, infrastructure and specialists' time.

332.title: How much a proprietary LLM costs: how to choose an approach and calculate the full cost of the product
332.short: A breakdown of industry practice in creating and using LLMs. The speaker shares a "ladder of options" and a transparent estimate for each scenario: using models via API, running an open model on your own infrastructure, adapting to a specific task or domain, a company's central model, proprietary pretrain and developing a frontier model. We break down which needs each scenario covers and which requirements really justify moving to a more complex solution. What each estimate consists of and the phasing method that allows buying step-by-step hypothesis checks with decision points.

How to build a portrait of a customer the bank does not yet have: which sources proved useful and which turned out to be noise.

335.title: The architecture of modern analytical realtime systems
335.short: A breakdown of a working realtime attribution system that we designed, brought to production load and measured ourselves, with numbers at every step: from 11 rows/s in staging to ~26 thousand events/s in production, with benchmarks of four databases and cost in rubles per million events. Attendees will take away not a list of technologies, but verifiable selection rules. We'll show not only the results but also our own mistakes in measurement methodology
335.description:
Building a mobile tracker capable of competing on equal terms with the global leaders of the attribution market requires an uncompromising architecture. The system must process tens of thousands of events per second, guarantee data consistency, and at the same time remain economically viable. The talk examines the engineering underside of the production realtime attribution system TraceHub, which was designed from scratch and brought to a load of 26,000 events per second. This is not a theoretical overview of technologies, but an honest breakdown of one production pipeline with concrete cost figures per million events at every stage.

The speaker will present the results of a direct benchmark of databases for the hot state on the same code (Cassandra vs ScyllaDB vs YugabyteDB vs YDB), clearly showing why transactionality can make a database 20 times slower for a specific task. You will learn how the three-tier storage architecture is built (Scylla for the hot state, ClickHouse exclusively for aggregates and Iceberg for eternal storage of raw logs), and what real price the business pays for quorum when reading from neighboring availability zones.

Separate attention will be paid to non-obvious optimization lessons. Kirill will break down why rewriting in Rust does not help if the business logic runs into waiting for the network, how the default 5 ms pause in Kafka ate up 28% of processing time, and how to properly build a ladder of retries and a DLQ (Dead Letter Queue) so as not to lose money on critical paths. Attendees will get a verifiable set of rules for designing high-load systems and metrics that allow finding real bottlenecks in the infrastructure.

338.title: We grew a junior. What next? How not to lose an analyst after the first successes
338.short: How to grow novice analysts so that they become independent faster, bring value to the product and do not lose interest in the work after the probation period. I'll share how we work with mistakes, questions, feedback and gradually transfer responsibility. And we'll talk about why even a well-trained junior may want to leave
338.description:
Hiring and onboarding junior analysts require huge investments of the mentor's and the team's time. However, a situation often arises when a technically trained specialist who has successfully passed the probation period suddenly loses motivation or leaves the company without having had time to recoup the resources invested in them. In the era of AI copilots, the value of basic SQL writing is trending toward zero, so the main challenge is to transform a newcomer from an operator of tools into an independent specialist who understands business context as quickly as possible. The talk examines the practical experience of Liga Stavok in building an analyst development path.

The speaker will break down real behavior patterns of novice specialists: from an avalanche of questions about every step to completely silencing problems. You will learn how mentors themselves unconsciously block the growth of juniors (when "it's easier to do the task yourself") and at what exact moment the motivation breaks. Separate attention will be paid to the mechanics of considerate feedback: how to discuss mistakes so that they accelerate the transfer of the area of responsibility, and how to build a step-by-step development plan for the first 90 days and the subsequent period.

Attendees will get a transparent framework for working with junior specialists. The talk will help leads and senior analysts reduce time spent on constant checks and micromanagement, correctly assess the effectiveness of onboarding (not only by the fact of closing the probation period, but also by the speed of transition to autonomous research) and retain grown talent within the team.

339.title: “LLM plumbing” – how to build working AI pipelines without leaks
339.short: Methods for working with sensitive data: what kinds of data exist, which methods suit each case, how to pick the right method, and where it can all break. We look at how (and what) not to let providers do with your data. A detailed discussion of how to use LLM in situations where a lot of sensitive data may be involved, and how to avoid leaks, reassure the security team, release the service, and not go broke on hardware. Listeners will get answers to the questions: how to use LLM effectively without training the provider, without breaking the law, without attracting regulators, and while staying friends with the security team; what to do if we want to run neural networks on our own (on-premise)? How to “manipulate” data to remove sensitivity while preserving the essence? How to stitch pipelines for the task, balancing privacy and power? How to create “blinders” for LLM so control is not handed to users?

340.title: Obfuscation of personal data — not a savior but a trap
340.short: The risks of modern personal data protection laws (GDPR, 152 FZ, CCPA, PDPA, PDPL, DPDPA) in the context of using external AI models. How legal is it to send personal data to external AI service APIs? How realistic is it to protect against risks through obfuscation of the data sent? We break down the risks, the opportunities, and the reliability of such protection
340.description: Integrating external AI services into business processes inevitably runs into the harsh reality of data protection legislation (GDPR, 152-FZ, CCPA, and similar). Trying to legitimately use cloud LLMs, many data teams resort to obfuscation or pseudonymization of datasets before sending them via API. It is commonly assumed that replacing names with hashes and hiding explicit identifiers reliably protects the business from regulators. The talk breaks down why this approach is a dangerous illusion that often does not withstand either technical or legal scrutiny.

341.title: Can this be sent to an LLM? Legal requirements of 152-FZ when working with foreign models
341.short: Where do personal data appear in an LLM product? How an external API, a Russian intermediary and self-hosting an open model differ. How to establish the actual recipients of data and the countries of processing. Legal grounds for processing, localization, notifications under Articles 12 and 22, contracts and the allocation of liability. What information you need to obtain from the vendor and what to do if it does not disclose the necessary terms. What happens to the legal status of data after full names and phone numbers are removed. How to account for indirect identification, a retained mapping table and the possibility of restoring information from context. Storage of requests and responses, use of data for training, employee access, engagement of other processors, deletion of information and actions in case of incidents. Walkthroughs of typical product scenarios and edge cases (for example, the model is hosted inside the company, but individual components — speech recognition, embedding generation or logging — use external services. How to assess the system as a whole in this case)

342.short: We discuss identifiability, bias and decision-making under uncertainty. 343.title: Growing Yggdrasil: how to build a working metric graph
343.short: The metric the business wants to influence and the metric the business can influence with an arbitrary action are usually different metrics. We look at how to build healthy iteration on product hypotheses using a metric graph. Listeners will learn how to extract more information from a set of experiments — what else can be learned about users by looking at the whole set of experiments — and how to measure and decompose the effect of a package of marketing changes on a business metric when no single experiment gives an answer on its own.
343.description:
The global metric the business wants to grow and the local metric the product team can actually influence with a direct action are almost always two different entities. The gap between high-level KPIs and the results of specific releases means that local experiments consistently show growth while the overall economics don't add up. The talk covers the methodology for building a metric graph that connects proxy indicators to the main business goal and sets up a healthy process of iterating on hypotheses.

The speaker will show how to move from evaluating isolated A/B tests to analyzing an entire ecosystem of experiments. You will learn how the architecture of nested metrics helps extract hidden insights about user behavior that are unavailable from a point look at raw data. Special attention will be paid to the math of the cumulative effect: Max will walk through the algorithm for measuring and decomposing the impact of a large set of marketing changes on the final business indicator.

Listeners will get a rigorous analytical framework for evaluating complex product initiatives. The talk will provide a clear toolkit for situations where no single test can give a mathematically reliable answer at the macro level, but the business needs to estimate the real effect of the entire set of launched changes.

344.title: Mutation testing for AI agents in A/B tests
344.short: A system of AI agents around the A/B platform and measuring its reliability via a benchmark based on mutation testing: we inject controlled defects into cases with a known answer and calculate mutation score, false positive rate, and the detection threshold. On this proving ground we compare models and architectures and determine the tolerance limits where agents can already be trusted
344.description:
Trust in AI agents working within the A/B experimentation platform cannot be built on blind faith. When LLMs help design tests or interpret their results, the price of an unnoticed hallucination is wrongly rolled-out functionality and lost money. The talk covers Cian's experience in building a system for objectively measuring the reliability of analytical AI agents using the mutation testing methodology.

The speaker will show the internal mechanics of the AI proving ground: how controlled defects and distortions (mutations) are deliberately introduced into historical A/B test cases with a known reference answer. You will learn how to mathematically assess the agent's ability to find these errors using rigorous metrics: mutation score, false positive rate (FPR), and the anomaly detection threshold.

Listeners will see how, on the basis of such a benchmark, various generative models and agentic pipeline architectures can be compared directly. The talk will give data scientists and platform engineers a verifiable framework for determining tolerance limits — an algorithm that makes it possible to mathematically prove exactly which tasks an AI agent can already be fully trusted with, and where mandatory human oversight is still required.

The talk is about the transition from manual task specifications to a self-service architecture. The speaker will show how an analyst can independently develop a typical loading flow and ship it to production without the platform team being involved at every stage. The solution is based on YAML configurations, automated release pipelines and AI-based generators. Special attention will be paid to the mechanics of working with the neural network: what data, rules and documentation from the catalog are fed into the model's context so that the algorithm helps write valid integration configurations rather than just answering empty prompts.

Listeners will see the real picture of working with generative AI in data engineering. The talk will show how to scale the onboarding of systems without a proportional growth in manual labor. You will get a transparent scheme of how responsibilities are split: which technical handovers disappear thanks to platform automation, and which decisions on understanding a source, describing objects and controlling data quality will always require an analyst's expertise.

347.title: A/B test interference: from myths to measurable results and understanding the scale of the problem
347.short: A complete interference model (distortion of a result due to overlapping experiments), an original criterion for assessing the influence of one experiment on another, and an internal tool for on-the-fly checking, from the ASL team that builds T-Bank's in-house A/B platform.
347.description:
More than 10 thousand experiments run at T-Bank every year, and many of them overlap. The question arises: can the results of such experiments be trusted, or does the overlap distort the effect (interference) and a retest is required? The question is especially acute, for example, in tests of marketing communication campaigns, where various pushes and SMS compete for the user's limited attention.

The topic has been hyped for a long time, and an experiment isolation system is an essential foundation of mature A/B platforms. Yet no one can articulate how to estimate the scale of the influence. Because of this, interference remains a semi-mythical problem: some ignore it entirely, others isolate part of the experiments based on expert judgment, and still others prefer to isolate almost everything, sacrificing the speed of running experiments.

At the same time, we built a complete mathematical model, derived an original criterion for assessing the influence of one experiment on another and developed an internal tool for on-the-fly checking.

Attendees will be introduced to the interference model, learn how to estimate it and what the size of the distortion depends on. We will share research results from T-Bank: we will answer the question of interference scale, show interesting cases and also share internal insights.

356.title: Fighting organic cannibalization and wrong optimization
356.short: We will reveal the technical side of building an end-to-end ROAS reporting system that tied ad network spend, clicks and revenue into a single loop, which allowed optimizing the performance budget by 30%. The report became a Single Source of Truth both for manual optimization by buyers and for automated agents that partially manage campaigns via API, which ultimately cut reaction time to drops from days to a couple of hours
356.description:
Blind traffic buying due to delayed conversions is the main pain of performance marketing. The situation is aggravated by the fact that unconditional trust in mobile tracker (MMP) reports regularly leads to wrong optimization: ad networks hide fraud, take credit for others' achievements and openly cannibalize organic traffic. As a result, the budget quietly drains into channels that deliver cheap registrations but show zero payback over distance. The talk breaks down the experience of the dating service Mamba in building end-to-end ROAS reporting infrastructure, which made it possible to cut the performance budget by 30% while maintaining target profit.

The speaker will reveal the technical underside of the analytical loop that tightly tied network spend, clicks and real user payments into a single Single Source of Truth. You will learn how to build cross-validation of tracker data and introduce hybrid purchase management: routine protection against waste is handed to external API agents that automatically switch off unprofitable creatives based on early payback predictions. This cut reaction time to traffic drops from several days to a couple of hours.

Listeners will get a framework proven at Highload scale for cleaning the funnel of inefficient traffic. The talk will help marketing leaders and analysts restructure buying processes so as to completely free the team from manual budget micromanagement, focusing buyers exclusively on scaling profitable bundles.

358.title: People management and project context: how a leader can keep the balance
358.short: As a team grows, people management takes up ever more of a leader's time and attention. Hiring, employee development and organizational issues push out project context — it becomes harder for the leader to discuss tasks substantively and offer meaningful solutions. 364.title: A/B test calculations for unusual metrics: MAU, WAU, Retention, NSAT, Contact Rate and CTR
364.short: Standard statistical tests do not work for complex product metrics (MAU, Retention, NPS, CTR) because of their ratio structure and autocorrelation, and bootstrap takes too much time. In the workshop we'll break down the creation of a fully autonomous pipeline for evaluating A/B experiments in pure SQL (Presto/Trino) without third-party platforms. Participants will get a ready algorithm and code: from setting up SRM control and linearizing metrics to calculating MDE with the Bonferroni correction and obtaining final p-values from raw logs.
364.description:
We'll show how to build a fully autonomous calculation of a split experiment for key product metrics — WAU, MAU, NSAT/NPS, Retention and Sticky Factor, Contact Rate and CTR — without involving third-party analytical platforms. Traditional z-test and t-test formulas work only for simple click-through conversions, applying bootstrap requires computation time, and linearization and the delta method need to be applied correctly. A product's key metrics (active users, satisfaction scores, contact coefficients) have internal connectivity, dependence, autocorrelation, low frequency or ratio structure, so without bringing them to a certain form they give false conclusions. Source audiences in the groups may differ when testing different entry points into conversion funnels, which leads to a bias in group volumes.

We'll show how to calculate MDE and sample size for different types of metrics — calculation taking into account the metric type (observation dependence, internal connectivity, bias) and the multi-group Bonferroni correction (α-adjust). SRM control — a fast χ² test in SQL that reveals a skew in the distribution of users between experimental groups. We'll write, in plain SQL, the linearization of ratio metrics (CTR, Contact Rate) and calculate a t-test on the transformed metrics. We'll show how to carry out a correct calculation for ordinal data (NSAT/NPS) and special conversion metrics like Retention and Sticky Factor. We'll show a pipeline in Presto/Trino — from the raw hits table to a ready VIEW with confidence intervals and p-values. We'll tell examples where we encountered metrics unusual in structure and small data volumes, and how we handled experiments with different group volumes when testing different entry points into the funnels of user paths.

365.title: Conversational AI on top of corporate BI: access rights, verified numbers and the new role of the analyst. The path to AI-native analytics
365.short: We have built a conversational AI assistant into everyday work: an employee asks about sales in plain words, by text or voice, and gets a chart or a numeric answer. Access rights are inherited from BI, the answer is verified by code, and next to each number sits its "passport" (period, filters, source). Using a mistake the model made, I will show how verification works, what we measure in the pilot and where the bot went wrong. And then — the move to AI-native analytics: executives work with data themselves, their questions accumulate in a knowledge base, the business maintains the metrics dictionary, and the analyst becomes the architect of a system that brings hypotheses
365.description:
In the classic paradigm, data specialists often turn into a "live interface" to BI system filters, serving executives' urgent requests before planning meetings. Attempts to replace them with language models directly carry the risks of hallucinations and leaks of trade secrets. The talk examines the experience of fashion retailer Artenecy in deploying a conversational AI assistant that works on top of the corporate warehouse on a principle of strict separation of responsibilities: the neural network only translates a business question into a query, while the calculations themselves happen exclusively on the side of verified marts.

The speaker will lay out the architecture of a secure AI layer. You will learn how to implement seamless inheritance of access rights from BI so that each employee receives only the slice of data they are allowed, without taking information outside the corporate perimeter. Separate attention will go to the mechanics of building trust: every answer comes with a "number passport" (period, filters, source), and programmatic verification by code blocks incorrect outputs. Using a real mistake by the model, it will be shown how the hallucination protection system works and how to properly set pilot quality metrics, moving away from abstract "accuracy".

Attendees will get a blueprint for moving to AI-native analytics, where the log of user questions becomes an automatic sensor of demand for new marts and the basis for a metrics dictionary. The talk will help data team leaders restructure processes so that the analyst stops being a courier delivering numbers and becomes the architect of a system that generates business hypotheses.

366.title: An experiment on trading service quality for money
366.short: Customer service quality is a manageable economic parameter, not just a set of operational SLAs. At T-Bank, a large-scale A/B test was run that abandoned a single support standard: different segments got austerity modes (ECO, −30% costs) and premium support (CX+, +70% costs). The experiment proved that investment in quality pays off far beyond the contact center: CX+ mode statistically significantly grows NPV, increases product utilization, and even reduces the share of loan delinquencies. We will break down the evaluation mechanics via LTV proxy metrics and show how to differentiate service so you can safely cut costs and maximize total profit
366.description:
Customer service is traditionally optimized by operational metrics: cost per contact, response speed (SLA), and the automation percentage. However, this approach ignores the real long-term economic value of service to the business. At T-Bank, they decided to test the hypothesis that support quality is not an abstract good but a manageable economic parameter that can and should be deliberately changed depending on the segment. The talk covers a large-scale experiment on abandoning a single service standard and moving to distributing quality based on expected return on investment (LTV).

The speaker will reveal the mechanics of differentiating service into three modes: strict ECO with a 30% cost reduction (more persistent bots, increased SLAs, and a focus on speed for unprofitable customers and “troublemakers”), standard BASE, and expensive CX+, where the cost of service grows by 70% due to priority, dedicated experts, and motivation for full problem resolution for newcomers and the upper mass segment. You will learn how to build a system of proxy metrics to assess the impact of such modes on long-term LTV, transactional activity, and retention.

The test results proved that investment in CX+ goes far beyond service indicators: segment-weighted NPV grew by 2.2%, activations of new products jumped (for example, MVNO issuances by 3.3% and credit cards by 2.2%), and even the probability of default decreased — customers with quality service statistically significantly less often go delinquent (the Roll Rate 0 share grew by 0.24 pp). Listeners will get an analytical framework for moving to the incremental value of service: how to safely save where it does not destroy LTV, and pour budgets into support where it brings multiple returns.

370.short: In a year, measurements of brand visibility in neural-network answers have gone from an experiment to a line in the media plan. In a year, measurements of brand visibility in neural-network answers have gone from an experiment to a line in the media plan. But there is still no single methodology: agencies, vendors and in-house teams define a mention differently, build the prompt sample differently, choose the number of runs differently and assess the stability of results differently.

On the panel we will compare the approaches of those who make, sell and buy these measurements.

We will look at which parameters can already be unified (and whether they can be at all), where methodological differences are fundamental, and what research on the stability of LLM answers can give practitioners.

The result is a draft methodological minimum for the market: a set of criteria for checking how well-founded the numbers in an AI visibility report are. We will put it together on the panel and publish it after the conference.

371.title: From source to insight: what an AI agent needs for its answers to be trusted

We will break down where the agent already replaces manual work, where it makes mistakes and how to verify its answer all the way down to the source table.
